milestones.title: Londinium founded
milestones.detail: The Romans establish a settlement at a crossing of the Thames; its earliest securely dated structure, a timber drain beside the main road, dates to 47 CE.

milestones.title: Razed in Boudica's revolt
milestones.detail: In 60 or 61 CE the Iceni under Boudica force the Romans to abandon the settlement, which is razed; it is rebuilt after the revolt is defeated.

milestones.title: London Wall built
milestones.detail: Around 200 a defensive wall about 2 miles long and up to 6 m high is built around the city, enclosing about 330 acres.

milestones.title: Roman city abandoned
milestones.detail: Roman administration collapses in the early 5th century; by 457 the walled city appears almost completely abandoned and stays empty for some 200 years.
milestones.source: Naismith, Rory (2019), Citadel of the Saxons, p. 42, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_London

milestones.title: Alfred the Great reoccupies the walled city
milestones.detail: Alfred re-establishes English control of London in 886 and repairs the Roman walls; the old city, now Lundenburh, again becomes the main site of population.

milestones.title: The Normans build the White Tower
milestones.detail: The Norman stone keep of the Tower of London is begun in 1078 and is probably complete by 1100.

milestones.title: Stone London Bridge completed
milestones.detail: The medieval stone bridge, under construction from 1176, is completed in 1209 and stands until 1831.

milestones.title: The Black Death
milestones.detail: Plague reaches London in 1348, killing 200 Londoners a day at its height; the population falls from 80,000-100,000 around 1300 to about 40,000 in 1377.

milestones.title: The Great Plague
milestones.detail: The last major plague epidemic kills an estimated 100,000 people, about a fifth to a quarter of London's population.

milestones.title: The Great Fire of London
milestones.detail: From 2 to 5 September 1666 fire guts the medieval City inside the Roman wall, destroying Old St Paul's, 87 parish churches and an estimated 13,200 houses.

milestones.title: First census counts over a million
milestones.detail: The first national census records 1,011,157 people in the area of today's Greater London.

milestones.title: First railway opens
milestones.detail: The London and Greenwich Railway, opened between 1836 and 1838, is the capital's first steam railway, carried entirely on a viaduct.

milestones.title: World's first underground railway
milestones.detail: The Metropolitan Railway opens on 10 January 1863 from Paddington to near Smithfield, the world's first passenger-carrying underground railway.

milestones.title: The Blitz
milestones.detail: German bombing from 7 September 1940 to 16 May 1941 kills over 30,000 Londoners and destroys many buildings.

milestones.title: Greater London created
milestones.detail: The county of Greater London is established on 1 April 1965, replacing the smaller County of London (1889-1965).

milestones.title: Summer Olympic Games
milestones.detail: London hosts the Summer Olympics; the main focus is a new 200-hectare Olympic Park on a former industrial site in Stratford, east London.

landmarks.name: London Wall (Roman city wall)
landmarks.source: Museum of London, 'London Wall', via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Wall
landmarks.note: Up to 6 m high and 2.5-3 m wide; point is the surviving section at Tower Hill.

landmarks.name: White Tower (Tower of London)
landmarks.source: Allen Brown & Curnow (1984), Tower of London, pp. 9-12, and Impey & Parnell (2000), via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Tower_(Tower_of_London)
landmarks.note: Begun 1078, probably complete by 1100; 27 m high at the southern battlements.

landmarks.name: Westminster Abbey
landmarks.source: Westminster Abbey, 'Dimensions of Westminster Abbey', http://www.westminster-abbey.org/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/86076/ABBEY-Dimensions-for-web-.pdf, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey
landmarks.note: Present church consecrated 1269; 31 m (101 ft) is the height of the nave. The western towers, added in the 1740s, are taller but no sourced figure was found.

landmarks.name: Old St Paul's Cathedral
landmarks.note: Completed in the mid-14th century. Spire height is traditionally given as 489 ft (149 m), with estimates from 140 m; the spire burned in 1561 and was not replaced, and the cathedral was destroyed in the Great Fire of 1666.

landmarks.name: Monument to the Great Fire of London
Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben), Palace of Westminster
landmarks.note: 316 ft. CTBUH lists the Palace of Westminster (1859) at 102.4 m.

landmarks.name: St Pancras station hotel (Midland Grand Hotel)
Tower Bridge
landmarks.note: 213 ft, the height given for the bridge towers.

notes: Start date: 47 CE is the earliest securely dated structure (a tree-ring-dated timber drain) and the date now usually given for the foundation; an older view places the origin in a military enclosure of the invasion year 43 CE, so the range is 43-50 CE. Roman and early-medieval population is poorly known. The 140 CE point is the midpoint of the published 30,000-60,000 range; the population may have fallen by as much as two-thirds after about 150. The 457 point is shown as zero to represent the documented abandonment of the walled city (not a count); nothing reliable was found for Lundenwic or for late Saxon and Norman London (about 600-1199), so there is a gap of over 700 years. Medieval and early-modern points are scholarly estimates (Chandler via Reba et al., and historians cited by Wikipedia) and differ between authors: for 1300 Chandler gives 45,000 where recent work gives 80,000-100,000; for 1377 the range is 40,000-50,000. They cover the continuous built-up area (City, Westminster, Southwark and suburbs) as each author defines it. From 1801 the figures are decennial census counts re-aggregated to the present Greater London area (about 1,570 km2), which was partly rural in the early 19th century, so the step from 676,000 (1750, built-up area) to 1,011,157 (1801) is partly definitional; Chandler's built-up-area figure for 1801 is 864,845. 1939 is an official estimate, not a census (none was held in 1941). Landmarks: tower heights and years from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center where listed; older monuments from Wikipedia articles, with the cited source named where there is one. Old St Paul's is shown with its spire until 1666 although the spire itself was lost in 1561. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Westminster Abbey's western towers, Victoria Tower completion date, Westminster Cathedral campanile, Battersea Power Station chimneys, Wembley Stadium arch, the Crystal Palace (1854-1936).
